units: a neighborhood has two distinct ways to put a request to a local authority
the first way rests on a document taken around for people to sign
this way calls for very little in the way of materials
the administration is obliged to keep the written request
a signed document reflects neither disagreement nor shading
the second way means gathering people in a hall open to all
the meeting lets opposing views answer each other directly
people who cannot travel are shut out of the meeting
background noise puts quiet speakers at a disadvantage
the two ways complete each other, one measuring the discontent and the other explaining it
text: A neighborhood that wants a local authority to listen has two very different routes open to it. The first is a written request, carried door to door for signatures. It costs almost nothing, it can be put together in one evening, and it leaves a paper record the administration is obliged to keep. Its weakness is that it says nothing back: a signed sheet shows no shading, and nobody argues an objection out on it. The second route is a meeting in a hall open to all comers. Everyone states a case, opponents answer each other directly, and a compromise often takes shape before the room empties. But a meeting shuts out anyone who cannot travel, and the background noise buries the quiet speakers. The two go together: signatures measure how wide the anger runs, and the meeting shows where it comes from.

units: a repair truck came regularly to the square of a very small village
the children arrived first, drawn by the noise and the smell of the workshop
people brought damaged objects, among them a seat and a faulty lamp
a woman insisted on keeping a coffee mill despite its condition
each owner told the story of how the object had broken
the craftsman listened without looking away from his cutting bench
the square emptied little by little while the craftsman packed his crates
the narrator reads in these visits the proof that nothing was thrown out without argument
text: Week after week the repair truck pulled up at the edge of the square, and the whole small village seemed to open at once. The children came first, drawn by the racket of the grinder and by the smell of hot metal. Then came the objects: a chair whose seat had given way, a lamp with a bare wire, a coffee mill its owner refused to give up. Then came the stories, because nobody left without saying where the crack had come from. The repairman listened without lifting his eyes from the cutting bench, nodding in the right places. When he shut his crates, the square emptied slowly, the way a hall empties once a concert has ended. What he carried off was not only a load of scrap metal. It was proof, renewed week after week, that nothing here was thrown out before somebody had spoken up for it.

units: preparation starts with an inventory of the water points and outlets available
a notice goes up at the entrance a week before the operation
this notice gives the time, the expected length and the equipment to bring
the division of tasks is written down the day before
the lane running along the building has to be checked clear of bins
the cleaning starts with the high parts and works down toward the ground
starting from the bottom would mean redoing part of the cleaning
the equipment is put away before the last break, while the volunteers are still there
a written record of the damage goes to the manager at the end
text: Before you run a cleaning day in a shared courtyard, walk the ground and note which taps and power outlets actually work. A week ahead, put a notice at the entrance giving the start time, how long the job should take, and what tools people ought to bring. The evening before, write the jobs down with a name beside each one, because spoken instructions get forgotten. On the day, gather the volunteers by the gate and check that the lane along the building is clear of bins. Start high, with gutters and ledges, then work down toward the ground. Do it the other way and you will clean the same surfaces twice. Put the equipment away before the last break, while the volunteers are still together. Finish by writing down the damage you found and handing that note to the building manager.

a temporary footbridge has cut the detours without ending the congestion
text: A retaining wall gave way at the end of the week in an old part of town, and the road serving the foot of the slope was shut at once. With no route to fall back on, traffic shifted onto a narrow lane where two buses cannot pass each other. People living nearby report the same delays over and over, along with a crush at the one stop still in service. When a public information meeting was announced, a crowd gathered outside a hall far too small to hold everyone who turned up. Technical services blame the collapse on seepage that had gone on for years and was made worse by weeks of steady rain. Repairs will take several weeks, since the ground has to be tested before a fresh footing can be poured. A temporary footbridge is now in place, which has cut the detours without clearing the congestion.

units: the reception hall is on the lower floor of a low building
the light comes from a grimy skylight
a single reception counter works behind a pane with a hole in it
the line stretches as far as the front door
people coming and going in search of a form cut across the line
the wait sets off arguments about who goes next
colored tokens are now handed out on arrival
a board announces the color being called and seats have been installed
the counter works at the same rate but the quarrels have almost stopped
text: The reception hall sits on the lower floor of a squat building, and its light comes from a grimy skylight overhead. A single counter is open, behind a pane of glass with a round hole cut in it. The line in front of it stretches all the way to the front door, and it keeps getting broken by people wandering off to hunt for a form. Waiting sours the mood: someone questions who was there first, someone accuses a newcomer of pushing in. Since last season the desk has handed out wooden tokens at the door, each one marked with a color. A board shows which color is being called, and benches have been lined up along the wall. People sit, watch the board, and stop watching one another. The counter works at the same speed it always did, but the arguments have all but stopped in that once noisy room.

units: the author disputes the idea that help between neighbors has disappeared
in the building of his childhood, tools were borrowed from the door across the hall
an older resident watched the children without being asked
in his present building, people pass on the stairs without speaking
that same building produced volunteers to repaint a bike room
a list of people willing to wheel the bins out was drawn up there
the author puts the change down to the channel used and not to selfishness
help now travels through written messages and a notice board
the author prefers reserved but reliable neighbors to nosy ones
text: People keep telling me that neighbors have stopped helping each other out. My answer is that the help has only changed shape. In the building where I grew up, you knocked across the hall to borrow a wrench, and the woman on the top floor watched the children without ever being asked. Where I live now, nothing like that happens. We pass one another on the stairs without a word. So what? That same staircase turned out two volunteers last season to repaint the bike room, and a list of people willing to wheel the bins out. The difference is not selfishness, it is the channel. Help used to depend on closeness. Now it travels through a written message and a board hung by the mailboxes. I will take reserved neighbors who show up when it matters over chatty ones who keep score.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)

a member holds that without her the funds and the projects would both be empty
text: Her whole office fits inside a cupboard, and once a week she pulls out of it a binder as thick as a brick. As treasurer of a neighborhood association, she takes in the dues, chases the members who forget, and writes every figure by hand before copying it into a spreadsheet. She bargains too: the loan of a room next door, a discount from a printer, a bill put off a month, the patience of an annoyed landlord. And she decides, because the spending competes for one small pot. Supplies for the sewing workshop, a repair to the copier, refreshments for the open meetings. She turns down the top post she is offered at every renewal, saying that accounts kept straight weigh more than a title. Without her, one member says while stacking chairs, the pot would be empty and so would the plans.

units: the opening of the performance looked unpromising
the stage held only a bare platform and mismatched seats
the amateur performers seemed tense
the first scene suffered from a script that was too written and badly embodied
the room settled when an actress picked up a fallen ring of keys without breaking her line
the show gained pace from that incident onward
short scenes followed one another and the poor set stopped being a problem
the closing sequence ran without speech and showed neighbors ignoring each other
the critic holds that the script has to be shortened
the critic reckons the company would deserve a bigger hall
text: Nothing at the start of the evening promised much: a bare stage, three mismatched chairs, amateur players visibly stiff with nerves. The opening scene suffered from a script that had been written rather than spoken, and the voices recited it instead of carrying it. Then the room went quiet on its own when one actress, playing a caretaker, dropped her ring of keys and picked it up without breaking off her line. From there the show found its pace. Short scenes followed one another, the weariness of some answering the stubbornness of others, and the poor set stopped mattering. The final sequence, played without a word, struck me as the truest of all: neighbors crossing paths in a stairwell and failing to recognize each other. The script needs tightening. The company deserves a bigger house.

units: the sender announces a water shutoff affecting two stairwells
the cut is planned for the following afternoon

the return of pressure will bring a loud purge that is harmless
a whistle from the water heater must be reported to the manager
the cost will be met by the shared contribution already paid
text: To everyone in the building: the water will be off in both stairwells tomorrow afternoon. The cause is a corroded shutoff valve in the basement whose handle no longer turns. Since that one part controls the whole riser, nothing can be done on the upper floors until it is replaced. The corrosion came from a slow leak that took a long time to spot, because it ran straight into a drain. So, in practical terms: fill two containers per household the night before, and close your own taps while the water is off, to avoid damage when the pressure comes back. The plumber expects a loud purge on start-up, since the air being pushed out will rattle the pipes, and that is harmless. If your water heater whistles afterward, report it at once. The cost is covered by the dues already collected.

units: the question asked concerns a rise in the members' annual contribution
current income no longer covers the upkeep of the hall
the treasurer finds the rise moderate but fears shutting out members of small means
the board proposes opening the hall to outside uses in return for payment
the quiet periods are what this opening targets
an unused hall costs as much as a used one
bookings would be handled by members taking turns
a single register would prevent conflicting commitments
a review would be discussed in a general meeting if income still fell short
the chosen answer combines a limited rise with partial letting
text: Should the annual membership fee go up? The question arises because the income no longer covers the upkeep of the hall. The treasurer answers that the rise would be a small one, but that it would push out the members who can least afford it. Is there another way? Yes, the board replies: open the hall to outside users in return for a payment. The quiet stretches of the calendar are what it has in mind. An empty room costs no less than a busy one. Who would handle the bookings? A desk staffed by members in turn, working from a single register so that nobody promises the same evening twice. And if the money still falls short? Any revision goes back to a general meeting rather than being settled by the board alone. The chosen answer pairs a limited rise with partial letting, which spreads the effort instead of loading it onto a few.
